messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Monique Carter was a 33-year-old African American woman who had worked for seven years as a park ranger, a role that had once fit her neatly: she knew the trails by feel, could read weather shifts in the trees, and took pride in being the person visitors turned to when they were lost, frightened, or simply tired. Before the loss, she had been steady and capable in ways that mattered to her and to her marriage; she and her husband had built their routines around her long hours outdoors and the satisfaction she took in the work. Then, without warning, her younger brother died unexpectedly after a brief, traumatic event that Monique described in a way that made clear how abruptly it had cut through ordinary life. She had spoken about being on duty when the call came, and about the moment afterward when details arrived in pieces too fast for her to arrange into anything bearable. What stayed with her was not a smooth story but fragments that would appear and vanish: a sudden image of her brother as she had last seen him, the sharp sense of where she was standing when she heard, and then the awful return of the fact that he was gone. When she tried to remember, it was, in her words, “like looking at photographs,” each image fixed and lifelike for a second before the next one came. At those moments, grief rushed over her so intensely that she felt unable to stay with the memory for long.

In the weeks and months that followed, Monique found herself trying to keep her mind occupied at all times. She filled every spare moment with work tasks, errands, cleaning, checking and rechecking schedules, anything that would prevent her from sitting still long enough for the memory to surface. She noticed that relaxing had started to feel dangerous. Sitting on the porch in the evening, lying down after work, or even letting herself drift while watching television could leave her suddenly flooded with the images and the grief, and so she avoided down time whenever she could. At home, she took on extra responsibilities and quietly gave up some that had mattered to her before, not because she no longer cared, but because doing less left too much room for what she was afraid would come next. She also began stepping back from parts of her ranger duties that felt most exposed to reminders, asking for different assignments when possible and arranging her days so she could move through the park with less chance of being caught off guard.

By the time she came for help, Monique described feeling constantly on edge. Her body, she said, stayed tense as if it were waiting for something to happen, even in places that were objectively safe. She felt strong waves of fear, anger, guilt, and shame that could arrive without warning and leave her raw and exhausted. Nights were especially hard. She had trouble falling asleep and often woke again before morning, her mind immediately alert for danger or for the return of the images. She would lie awake listening to her own breathing and feeling the muscles in her shoulders and jaw locked tight, unable to settle. The emotional change troubled her almost as much as the intrusive recollections. Monique had come to believe that she was not the person she used to be. She told her therapist that she felt dead inside, as if some essential part of her had been taken with her brother, and that she had permanently changed for the worse. The qualities that once defined her—dependability, calm under pressure, the ability to lead—no longer felt available to her. At work, this left her troubled by tasks she had once managed effortlessly, and she worried each time she had to make a decision in front of others.

Her husband had noticed that she was harder to reach and that she seemed to be living at a distance even while sitting beside him. Monique did not describe dramatic outbursts so much as a flattening and withdrawal, punctuated by moments when the memory would break through and leave her shaken. What finally brought her to seek treatment was the strain of keeping everything going while feeling increasingly unable to rest or feel like herself. She was afraid that if she stopped moving, the photographs in her mind would return and the grief would overwhelm her again, but she was also frightened by how much life she was losing in the effort to stay away from them. She came hoping she could sleep, work, and be with her husband without feeling constantly braced for impact, and most of all she hoped she might find some way to hold her brother in mind without feeling that it would destroy her.
